title: Jason Calacanis on angel investing: small bets, performance over pitch, pre-emptive follow-ons
summary: Jason explains how he approaches early-stage investing: make many small bets, judge founders on performance and customer love rather than charisma, and pre-emptively fund winners to raise ownership. He also argues family offices should avoid passed-over seed deals or hire a dedicated investor, and covers remote work economics and consumerized enterprise software.

principles.text: Judge founders on performance and customer love, not charisma; talk to their customers.
principles.quote: the number one thing you should do that you are not doing and you're not doing it let's be honest is to talk to customers of that product

principles.text: Entry valuation matters: lower prices let you take more shots on goal for the same capital and ownership.
principles.quote: be valuation conscious it actually matters your entry point

principles.text: Preemptively fund your own breakout winners to raise ownership instead of waiting for them to go to market.
principles.quote: we're preemptively funding our own winners then we move from you know a six percent ownership percentage to a twelve to twenty percent ownership percentage

principles.text: Early-stage investing is a power-law game: most bets go to zero, so make many bets and double down on the breakouts.
principles.quote: it takes to win is being able to have proprietary deal flow make a lot of bets identify which ones are breaking out and then 10x seeing down on them

principles.text: Have a real edge. Family offices seeing deals only after top VCs passed are getting the leftover hands; prefer later-stage companies with revenue or back proven fund managers.
principles.quote: make sure that this company has not been passed on by everybody else because then you're just trying to split the arrow

principles.text: Be relentlessly helpful to everyone; that is how access to great deals like Uber happened.
principles.quote: if you just are a person who's helpful and you're helpful to everybody you meet like many people in Silicon Valley where to me and I probably wasn't the easiest person to be helpful to at times you're gonna have a great career
